paraphrase: Some wrong-viewed people say that inference is not a means of knowledge — yet in saying so with words they convey their intention, which is itself known by inference.
notes: Reported by an opponent: Śāntarakṣita, Tattvasaṅgraha (Buddhist). TS 1456 with Pañjikā ('some = the Bārhaspatyas and others'), checked.

paraphrase: The Lokāyata case: if no continuing entity exists, there is no other world, for there is no one to go there; body, mind and senses perish every moment and nothing else is admitted; therefore from particular elements, as the power of fermented liquor, cognition is produced or manifested; the elements in a particular arrangement are called body and senses, and there is no other principle; cognitions in different bodies are not cause and effect; the dying mind of one with passion does not link to another mind; so 'cognition arises from the body alone, sustained by in-breath and out-breath' — as Kambalāśvatara said.

paraphrase: Śāntarakṣita refutes the Lokāyata: cognition in the embryo is not absent; a cognition arises only from a preceding cognition of the same kind, so the first cognition of a life presupposes a former one; the body is not the material cause of mind; passion and the rest come from prior habituation; hence mind is a beginningless continuum and there is another world.
speaker: Śāntarakṣita
notes: Chapter end checked at v. 1964; the argument is summarised, verse-level refs not given.

paraphrase: In the examination of one who sees supersensible things, the Mīmāṃsā denial of an omniscient being is answered: the Buddha's omniscience is possible because the mind, freed by cultivation of selflessness from the afflictions, can know all; the Veda has no authority without a trustworthy speaker.

In the examination of the self, the selves of the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Sāṃkhyas, Jains, Upaniṣadic thinkers and Vātsīputrīyas are set out and refuted; the Upaniṣadic single eternal consciousness is rejected because cognitions are many and momentary, though their view is said to be close to the truth in holding consciousness to be the reality.
notes: Chapter-level summary; the remark that the Aupaniṣadas err only slightly is from memory (low).

paraphrase: In the examination of Īśvara, a permanent creator is refuted: an eternal cause would produce all its effects at once or never, and if it depends on auxiliary causes it is not the cause; the order of the world is explained by karma and conditions.

In the examination of the Lokāyata, the materialist denial of other worlds is refuted: consciousness cannot arise from the body alone, for each moment of awareness arises from a preceding moment of awareness, so the series continues beyond death.

In the examination of the Word-brahman Śāntarakṣita argues that an eternal, single Word-brahman cannot account for successive and various things: if the world were its transformation it would be non-eternal and many; if it were only its appearance, the appearance would be unreal and the Word-brahman unproved; and no means of knowledge shows that cognition is interwoven with words.
notes: Argument summarized from memory; verse numbers not fixed.
